title: How the job is composed
description: Explore the same frozen skill composition, its proposed changes and source evidence using reusable HTML islands.
note: Current source d9e717b677e2ba32ad5c38896b5e6802ee029ed6. Proposed: Current source d9e717b6 (PR #132) · Proposed: phase composition spec v1 at 789e0ef0 · spec reviewed · not implemented — https://github.com/ShravanSunder/sunstack/blob/789e0ef040865c62a016b3d9ca6d79ce1683deea/docs/wip/skills-authoring/2026-10-15-phase-principle-composition/proposal.md. Skill descriptions are frontmatter claims; the proposed shared procedure's description comes from the proposal. A shared procedure is a reference file, not a skill. Roles describe responsibility context, not execution order. Orchestrators are deferred. Relationship colors describe target kinds; PROPOSED is a separate status. This is authored branch source, not an installed or behavior-tested release. A declared relationship does not prove a runtime load, assignment or usefulness.

nodes.label: debug-investigation
nodes.description: Use when investigating bugs, failing tests, flaky behavior, crashes, regressions, build failures, unexpected behavior, long-running monitor/watch requests, or requests to debug/root-cause a problem before implementing fixes.

nodes.label: discuss-clarify-mental-models
nodes.description: Use when shared understanding may have drifted (repeated corrections, hollow agreement, a term meaning two things) or the user asks to reconverge, share understanding, reflect back, or re-anchor. Not for artifact edits, review, evidence gathering, or first-pass extraction.

nodes.label: discuss-pathfinding
nodes.description: Use when requirements, user needs, domain terms, tacit process, or owner tolerances are unwritten and must be drawn out of someone's head: "grill me", "interview me", "help me figure out what I actually want". Not for authoring from settled sources.

nodes.label: docs-maintain
nodes.description: Use when updating, cleaning up, reconciling, archiving, or promoting project docs (AGENTS.md, README, changelogs, runbooks, architecture docs, workflow artifacts) from settled code or decisions. Not for authoring unsettled spec or design meaning.

nodes.label: implement-plan
nodes.description: Use when executing or continuing one ready canonical implementation plan whose delivery context authorizes implementation, or correcting one implementation-owned review finding. Not for plan or design defects, independent review, or PR work.

nodes.label: implementation-handoff
nodes.description: Use when packaging implementation state for another agent, reviewer, CLI, or future session: a copy-paste blurb, reviewer prompt, Claude/Gemini/Codex handoff, unfinished-work handoff, or post-implementation review packet.

nodes.label: implementation-pr-wrapup
nodes.description: Use when pushing, opening, updating, monitoring, or finishing a GitHub pull request after implementation: its description, checks, comments, review threads, mergeability, or "merge when ready". Not for fresh code review (implementation-review).

nodes.label: implementation-review
nodes.description: Use when independently reviewing implemented code, proof, a branch diff, commit, PR head, or one bounded remediation before PR readiness, including when governing inputs are missing or conflicting. Not for design review (spec-program-review).

nodes.label: ops-linear-tracking
nodes.description: Use when the user asks to create, organize, update, delete, or inspect Linear projects, milestones, issues, dependencies, ticket breakdowns, blocked/unblocked work, or tickets generated from architecture docs.

nodes.label: ops-observability-stack
nodes.description: Use when starting, checking, using, debugging, or verifying the shared local OpenTelemetry and Victoria stack for AgentStudio, Agent VM, OpenClaw, beta apps, debug apps, or any repo that emits OTLP locally.

nodes.label: ops-security-review
nodes.description: Use when the user asks for a security scan, security audit, threat model, vulnerability review, security diff scan, or remediation of one security finding.

nodes.label: plan-handoff
nodes.description: Use when packaging an existing implementation plan for another agent, CLI, machine, or future session, especially when the user asks for a copy-paste prompt, next-agent context, or portable plan packet.

nodes.label: plan-implementation
nodes.description: Use when writing or revising a repository-grounded implementation plan from reviewed Requirements, Specification, and Program Design, an admitted improvement finding, or a direct planning request. Not for audit-only discovery (plan-improve-repo).

nodes.label: plan-improve-repo
nodes.description: Use when auditing a repository for improvement opportunities, backlog-worthy refactors, quality gaps, or leverage points and turning admitted findings into implementation plans. Not for planning directly from a reviewed design (plan-implementation).

nodes.label: practices-collaboration
nodes.description: Use at the start of a qualifying task to find the repository's board project and work thread, and whenever agents coordinate: messaging or commissioning a session, seats, message or post, waiting on another agent, or no board. Not for tool syntax.

nodes.label: practices-manage-agents
nodes.description: Use when delegating to subagents, agent teams or parallel agents: the Lead or an authorized helper chooses an Advisor, Implementer, Verifier, Reviewer, Researcher or Operator, its valid Worker or Sidekick form, and model; or spawns, commissions, continues, steers, waits for, monitors, verifies or assesses that work, including a fan-out across many units. Not for performing the assigned engineering phase itself.

nodes.label: practices-research
nodes.description: Use when a task needs source gathering, prior-art research, current docs or web evidence, or memory, session-log, or saved-reader research before design, planning, review, or discussion can continue. Not for extracting unwritten owner meaning.

nodes.label: practices-show-me-your-work
nodes.description: Use at the start of a qualifying task to open or resume the work trace; while one is open, to record a decision, evidence, blocker, or outcome or to hand off; or when the user asks to show your work or for a trail. Not for routine small edits.

nodes.label: presentation-tui
nodes.description: Use when composing a substantial architecture, comparison, tradeoff, flow, or multi-section response, or when putting a design decision in front of the owner, on a monospace terminal or CLI host, or when the host is unknown: "draw this out", "compare these". Not for rendered chat (presentation-webui).

nodes.label: presentation-webui
nodes.description: Use when composing a substantial architecture, comparison, tradeoff, flow, or multi-section response, or when putting a design decision in front of the owner, on a rendered markdown chat host (Cursor chat, Claude.ai, ChatGPT): "draw this out", "compare these". Not for a monospace CLI (presentation-tui).

nodes.label: principle-build-the-shared-model-first
nodes.description: Use when about to build on someone else's picture (a request, a spec, a resumed plan, another agent's handback), or when agreement on something complex comes too fast. Form your own picture, restate it specifically enough to be corrected, and settle the gaps before building.

nodes.label: principle-define-the-domain-first
nodes.description: Use when a new noun, state, or stored field appears, one word is doing two jobs, or two sources use different words for what may be one thing. Define what each term means, what makes two of them the same, and what changes its state, before choosing structure.

nodes.label: principle-design-for-concurrency
nodes.description: Use when actors already overlap: two workers, retries, callbacks, background tasks, or late results can touch the same resource. Name the invariant, find the interleaving that breaks it, isolate the shared state before serializing it, and order by causal signals, not sleeps.

nodes.label: principle-design-for-failure
nodes.description: Use when a call, job, or state change has an effect someone else can see and it can time out, be retried, partly succeed, or end without you knowing. Decide every ending, which system is the truth for 'did it happen?', and who cleans up, before choosing retries or locks.

nodes.label: principle-experiment-before-proposing
nodes.description: Use when running something would settle a question faster than arguing about it: an unknown API behavior, a performance claim, which of two designs works better, how a prompt or classifier performs. Capture a baseline, fit the rigor to the stakes, and measure the real artifact.

nodes.label: principle-hold-the-scope
nodes.description: Use when a new request arrives, a design or plan comes back from someone else, or work is about to be called done. State who it is for, what success looks like, and what stays out; then check that every owner line is carried, nothing is invented, and nothing is weakened.

nodes.label: principle-justify-the-complexity
nodes.description: Use when adding or keeping a layer, abstraction, option, mechanism, or second path, or when sequencing a refactor or rewrite. Double-check that each piece of complexity is justified by an outcome that needs it now; remove the rest and cut over completely.

nodes.label: principle-name-the-tradeoffs
nodes.description: Use when a real choice changes complexity, risk, cost, or reversibility, or when one option is presented for a decision that has others. Show the credible alternatives as changes to the current design, with concrete gains, costs, who pays, and the assumption that must hold, then recommend one.

nodes.label: principle-one-owner-per-truth
nodes.description: Use when truth, effects, or guarantees cross a boundary: two parts can write the same state, a copy holds data another part owns, a schema is defined twice, or stored data starts to mean something new. Give each truth one authoritative owner and state what callers may rely on.

nodes.label: principle-prove-it-works
nodes.description: Use when about to say a feature, fix, or UI change works. A passing test proves only what it observes: proof is the feature working through the real entry point, observed where the user would see it, with anything unverified named.

nodes.label: principle-read-ground-truth-first
nodes.description: Use when about to claim what current code, a system, a document, or a library does, or to explain an unexpected behavior. Read the decisive source and the whole artifact, trace the real path, and label every claim as seen, inferred, or guessed.

nodes.label: principle-refine-mental-models
nodes.description: Use when reality surprises the plan, a fix fails twice on the same premise, or the same correction comes twice. Stop and ask what was wrong with the understanding before touching the code: drift or a break, and which shared premise to attack.

nodes.label: principle-separate-the-concerns
nodes.description: Use when adding a module, layer, interface, or dependency, when one part changes for two unrelated reasons, or when testing one rule drags in the network, the clock, or the framework. Give each part one job and inject dependencies at real seams.

nodes.label: principle-types-are-communication
nodes.description: Use when designing or reviewing types, signatures, or data that crosses a boundary (network, file, environment, database, model output), especially status fields, ids, and optional fields that only make sense together. Model states as sum types, build valid shapes, parse once at the boundary, and handle every variant.

nodes.label: principle-verify-before-accepting
nodes.description: Use when accepting any result: a helper's handback, a review finding, a passing run, 'done', an agreement, or your own conclusion. Check that this evidence establishes this exact claim, at this version, observed rather than reported, and name what it doesn't cover.

nodes.label: principle-write-for-the-reader
nodes.description: Use when writing a design, code, an instruction, or an explanation someone else must follow: a reviewer, a future maintainer, another agent, the owner tomorrow. Write so a reader with no context can answer their question quickly, restate the point, and find where to correct it.

nodes.label: principle-write-tests-that-can-fail
nodes.description: Use when writing, changing, or keeping a test for a fix, a feature, or a refactor, or when a claim rests on tests passing. Name the wrong behavior the test must catch, take the expected value from somewhere independent, run it at the cheapest layer where that wrong behavior can make it fail, and see it fail for the right reason.

nodes.label: program-design
nodes.description: Use when defining or revising structural How and its views: binding Specification entities to owners, homes, and schemas, then components, interfaces, state, flows, failure, trust boundaries, and proof seams. Not for defining what entities mean or other Why/What (spec-design).

nodes.label: spec-design
nodes.description: Use when authoring or revising durable Requirements from settled meaning, or a Specification's observable obligations, domain entities, and coverage views. Not for eliciting genuinely unwritten owner meaning (discuss-pathfinding).

nodes.label: spec-handoff
nodes.description: Use when packaging spec, design, architecture, or product-decision context for another agent, CLI, machine, or future session before an implementation plan exists.

nodes.label: spec-program-review
nodes.description: Use when independently reviewing a Specification, Program Design, or Requirements, Specification, and Program Design set, including reader understanding or readability, or deciding if a spec-only or program-only change needs review. Not for implementation review.

nodes.label: role-advisor
nodes.description: Use when a Lead commissions you as the Advisor Sidekick to challenge a design or an acceptance argument with a competing picture and tradeoffs. Not for the owner's main conversation, governing authorship or independent review findings.

nodes.label: role-implementer
nodes.description: Use when commissioned as the Implementer for approved changes, product tests, associated proof and corrections. Not for defining the governing outcome, observing as the paired Verifier or independent review.

nodes.label: role-lead
nodes.description: Use when you are the owner's main engineering partner responsible for governing design, plans, integration and acceptance. Not for a helper assigned bounded evidence, implementation, observation or independent review.

nodes.label: role-operator
nodes.description: Use when assigned as the Operator for prescribed execution, watch, scraping, extraction or guided collection under supplied criteria. Not for choosing engineering probes, synthesizing conclusions or repairing failures.

nodes.label: role-researcher
nodes.description: Use when assigned as the Researcher responsible for a checked answer to a bounded question or continuing investigation. Not for prescribed extraction alone, governing design authorship or delivery acceptance.

nodes.label: role-reviewer
nodes.description: Use when commissioned as an independent Reviewer for a declared artifact or its corrections, with no authoring history. Not for authoring, implementation or substituting advice for independent findings.

nodes.label: role-verifier
nodes.description: Use when commissioned as the paired Verifier to challenge proof feasibility, observe the adopted outcome or maintain assigned verification drivers. Not for product repairs, product-test authorship or acceptance.

nodes.label: review-proof-command-execution
nodes.description: Proposed shared procedure for running a review's granted proof commands: resolve the command chain, run only the exact granted commands, stop tracked or unknown writes, capture output and exit status, compare worktree status before and after, and report what could not run. It returns observations to the review lane, never a verdict.

edges.use: Work like a colleague at a whiteboard. The user holds one picture, you hold another; the job is to draw both pictures next to each other so the splits are visible, then settle each split with evidence or a question. sources.text: Missing evidence is `unverified`, not rejection. A category name is not an anchor: "the reliability requirement" fails the anchor fields until the exact governing clause is opened and quoted; a candidate whose anchor fields cannot be filled from an inspectable source is `unverified` or routes to an owner decision, never `accepted`. A candidate is a mental-model break — not an ordinary design finding — when its correction cannot be expressed inside the current governing basis because an assumption the basis itself relies on is false (the design assumes an interface, ordering, ownership, or guarantee the current system does not provide); a defect the basis already forbids and can name the fix for routes to its semantic owner as usual, while a break returns `decision-needed` or `blocked` to the owner instead of consuming a correction round. Weigh the dispel check's classifications and over-delivery map as candidate evidence like any other check result, and quote the rail text when overriding its class. A reviewer candidate that adds unrequested scope is `rejected: scope expansion` (an observation for the owner, not a decision the owner owes); an `absent`-mapped design element already in the artifacts is never rejected as harmless — it returns `decision-needed` (deletion recommended) or an accepted removal routed to `program-design`. An accepted finding names the unrealized obligation and its failure, never the reviewer's proposed mechanism. Style preference without reader or behavior effect is rejected. Before accepting missing contracts on a proposed mechanism, test whether deleting the mechanism preserves every confirmed requirement. Prefer deletion when it does. The 🔎 Reviewer Sidekick opens the source anchors from its bounded lookup before disposition. A reviewer concern that cannot be tied to an accepted requirement and observable failure is advice awaiting investigation, not implementation authority.

edges.label: applies judgment
edges.why:
Finding the ordering that breaks the invariant and removing unsafe sharing without discarding useful parallelism.

Explanation of a declared source relationship; no runtime loading claim
edges.when: Conditional · The source clause below owns the condition; a mention alone does not make this an unconditional load.
edges.use: **The wrong behavior sets the floor: what must stay real.** Keep real the smallest thing responsible for it. "The pricing rule rounds wrong" needs only the rule. "The serialized event drops a field" needs the real serializer and the real consumer's validation, not a live socket; the transport stays real only when delivery, ordering, or recovery is the claim. "The transaction doesn't commit" needs the real database, and "the worker doesn't stop" the real worker. When the wrong behavior is a race, the interleaving must be real too; a test that runs the steps one after another has none (see `principle-design-for-concurrency`). A double that replaces the interaction you are claiming leaves it unproven, however green the test.

edges.use: **The wrong behavior sets the floor: what must stay real.** Keep real the smallest thing responsible for it. "The pricing rule rounds wrong" needs only the rule. "The serialized event drops a field" needs the real serializer and the real consumer's validation, not a live socket; the transport stays real only when delivery, ordering, or recovery is the claim. "The transaction doesn't commit" needs the real database, and "the worker doesn't stop" the real worker. When the wrong behavior is a race, the interleaving must be real too; a test that runs the steps one after another has none (see `principle-design-for-concurrency`). A double that replaces the interaction you are claiming leaves it unproven, however green the test.

sources.text: Missing evidence is `unverified`, not rejection. A category name is not an anchor: "the reliability requirement" fails the anchor fields until the exact governing clause is opened and quoted; a candidate whose anchor fields cannot be filled from an inspectable source is `unverified` or routes to an owner decision, never `accepted`. A candidate is a mental-model break — not an ordinary design finding — when its correction cannot be expressed inside the current governing basis because an assumption the basis itself relies on is false (the design assumes an interface, ordering, ownership, or guarantee the current system does not provide); a defect the basis already forbids and can name the fix for routes to its semantic owner as usual, while a break returns `decision-needed` or `blocked` to the owner instead of consuming a correction round. Weigh the dispel check's classifications and over-delivery map as candidate evidence like any other check result, and quote the rail text when overriding its class. A reviewer candidate that adds unrequested scope is `rejected: scope expansion` (an observation for the owner, not a decision the owner owes); an `absent`-mapped design element already in the artifacts is never rejected as harmless — it returns `decision-needed` (deletion recommended) or an accepted removal routed to `program-design`. An accepted finding names the unrealized obligation and its failure, never the reviewer's proposed mechanism. Style preference without reader or behavior effect is rejected. Before accepting missing contracts on a proposed mechanism, test whether deleting the mechanism preserves every confirmed requirement. Prefer deletion when it does. The 🔎 Reviewer Sidekick opens the source anchors from its bounded lookup before disposition. A reviewer concern that cannot be tied to an accepted requirement and observable failure is advice awaiting investigation, not implementation authority.

tables.title: Proposed phase decomposition · nine phases
tables.description: Current source d9e717b6 (PR #132) · Proposed: phase composition spec v1 at 789e0ef0 · spec reviewed · not implemented · Spec reviewed · not implemented. Shared procedure is a reference file, not a skill.

cells.text: R1 · Derive meaning using the domain principle
Identity, relationship and state extraction → define-the-domain-first
Entity table with stable E ids, source selection, reuse of authoritative terms, settled-versus-unmade gap and route
R2 · Boundaries and complexity earn their place
Boundary choice → separate-the-concerns · necessity test → justify-the-complexity · coexistence only under an authorized external constraint
Entity bindings, shapes, owners, interfaces, dependency rules, diagrams, requirement coverage, structural-realization confirmation, migration phase fields
R3 · Plan tests that can disprove the claim
Honest layer, independent oracle, removal grounds → write-tests-that-can-fail
Slice proof map, project layer source, property or example choice, keep/repair/remove with removal evidence, integration gates, split and replan stops
R4 · Accept candidates, then plan their real proof
Candidate vetting → verify-before-accepting · proof that can fail → write-tests-that-can-fail
Opened anchors, rejected/unknown dispositions, admission variants, plan-only versus delivery, separate current-state receipt, immutable canonical plan
R5 · Produce proof and classify surprises
Choosing the real observation → prove-it-works · what a surprise means → refine-mental-models
Proof report, slice gate, five result classes with exact routes, scope and authority branches
R6 · Ground causal claims and reconsider failed premises
Locating the real divergence → read-ground-truth-first · repeated failed fixes → refine-mental-models
Bug packet, reproduction classification, evidence for and against, smallest discriminating step, artifact rules, monitoring
R7 · Compose judgment and extract common command execution
Necessity → justify-the-complexity · candidate disposition → verify-before-accepting · finding versus broken premise → refine-mental-models · command running → shared procedure
Rails, complete diff and chunk coverage, dispositions, result precedence, convergence; the proof lane keeps claim selection, interpretation, its one diagnostic rerun and its status
R8 · Consume the same execution procedure, keep design judgment
Same three judgments as R7 · failure and concurrency only inside the selected risk lane · command running → shared procedure

Mode admission, semantic coverage, structural-realization confirmation, ordered routes, bounded correction policy; the proof lane keeps its narrower claim predicate and its rerun-comparison result, and does not inherit implementation review's automatic one-rerun rule
R9 · Assess readiness evidence at its actual gate
Gate-to-observation comparison → verify-before-accepting
Live head, base, body, checks, threads and mergeability queries, public safety, final re-fetch, explicit merge authority, monitor behavior

sources.text: Missing evidence is `unverified`, not rejection. A category name is not an anchor: "the reliability requirement" fails the anchor fields until the exact governing clause is opened and quoted; a candidate whose anchor fields cannot be filled from an inspectable source is `unverified` or routes to an owner decision, never `accepted`. A candidate is a mental-model break — not an ordinary design finding — when its correction cannot be expressed inside the current governing basis because an assumption the basis itself relies on is false (the design assumes an interface, ordering, ownership, or guarantee the current system does not provide); a defect the basis already forbids and can name the fix for routes to its semantic owner as usual, while a break returns `decision-needed` or `blocked` to the owner instead of consuming a correction round. Weigh the dispel check's classifications and over-delivery map as candidate evidence like any other check result, and quote the rail text when overriding its class. A reviewer candidate that adds unrequested scope is `rejected: scope expansion` (an observation for the owner, not a decision the owner owes); an `absent`-mapped design element already in the artifacts is never rejected as harmless — it returns `decision-needed` (deletion recommended) or an accepted removal routed to `program-design`. An accepted finding names the unrealized obligation and its failure, never the reviewer's proposed mechanism. Style preference without reader or behavior effect is rejected. Before accepting missing contracts on a proposed mechanism, test whether deleting the mechanism preserves every confirmed requirement. Prefer deletion when it does. A reviewer concern that cannot be tied to an accepted requirement and observable failure is advice awaiting investigation, not implementation authority.

cells.text:
Evidence versus adopted authority
PROPOSED · Strengthen existing method
→ practices-research for tracing; principle-hold-the-scope for authority
Existing owners; ground truth obtains evidence and verification judges claim support

Researcher charter: pasted proposal versus owner adoption
Specification / Pathfinding: normative source classification
Docs maintenance: current source versus intended behavior

Several roles and phases repeat the distinction between what a source shows and what authorizes a requirement. Share source tracing and authority judgment, while retaining each phase's different application.
When: A consequential conclusion depends on source context, authorship, adoption, version or an indirect summary.
Use: Read surrounding context and return separate observation and authority anchors. Use scope judgment when material becomes a normative obligation; ordinary factual transcription needs no extra authority exercise.

Researcher retains the checked answer and short case. Specification retains normative derivation; Pathfinding confirms owner meaning; Docs keeps maintenance classification; Lead retains governing decisions.
Failure: A user message quoting an agent proposal is treated as the owner's requirement.
Valid control: Explicit scoped owner adoption is accepted without asking again or rejecting it because an agent suggested it first.

sources.label: roles/researcher.md:7
sources.text: **Case:** an Operator marks an "owner prompt" that contains pasted agent text as an owner requirement. Read the surrounding source: authorship alone is not adoption. Keep explicit owner decisions, established contracts and independently demonstrated constraints separate from agent proposals. **Clean case:** the owner expressly adopts the proposal in context. Keep it; an agent suggesting it first is no reason to reject it.

sources.label: spec-design/SKILL.md:25
sources.text: Two judgments carry the work. The first is legitimacy: every normative statement traces to an owner decision or a binding contract. A well-argued proposal, the current code, and your own restatement of the owner are not decisions. The second is precision: for each obligation, picture the cheapest implementation that satisfies its words. If that implementation could still miss the outcome the owner wants, the words are wrong, and you rewrite them until it fails.

sources.label: principle-hold-the-scope/SKILL.md:19
sources.text: **Trace every line to its source.** For each requirement or design element, ask where it came from. There are three answers: the owner asked for it; a constraint forces it (a contract, a law, behavior that must not break, a demonstrated technical limit); or it seemed like a good idea. The third kind is a question for the owner, not a requirement: "This version gate came from our draft, not from you or a protocol, so it can't be required behavior." A spec or plan an agent wrote is not, on its own, evidence of what the owner wants, so a line being in a document doesn't make it authorized. This applies to outcomes, behavior, exclusions, and obligations: the things the owner will judge. A build choice that changes none of those (a function name, an internal structure, how pull requests are grouped) is yours to make; decide it, record why, and keep moving.

sources.label: practices-research/SKILL.md:25
sources.text: 5. Verify load-bearing claims against primary sources, compare stale memory with live files, and surface contradictions or competing hypotheses. IF a conclusion is load-bearing or embeds the user's own hypothesis, the assignment owner may commission or resume one independent 🔎 Reviewer Sidekick through `practices-manage-agents`. IF the countercheck is commissioned, MUST load `references/countercheck.md` for its handoff and return per-claim `complete | partial | blocked` results before synthesis. Otherwise record why it was not selected.

cells.text:
Independent oracle and cheapest honest test layer
PROPOSED · Reuse existing principle
→ principle-write-tests-that-can-fail
Existing principle; reduce repeated general tutorials, keep applied methods

Verifier charter: testing pyramid
Test Design: minimum real interaction
Planning / implementation review: oracle and proof layer

The same general oracle/layer judgment is re-taught in roles and delivery phases. Its existing principle already owns it; the caller should apply it to its different planning, execution or assessment result.
When: Choosing or judging test placement, an expected value, or whether a double removes the interaction being claimed.
Use: Return the concrete wrong behavior, independent expected result, interaction that must remain real and cheapest honest layer. Short local applications consume the principle rather than reproduce its tutorial.

Planning keeps obligation-to-slice proof mapping; Test Design keeps scenarios; Implementer executes product tests; Reviewer inspects assertions; Verifier assesses delivered evidence and owns only granted drivers.
Failure: The expected serialized message is computed by the same serializer under test, or a fake erases the real routing defect.
Valid control: A literal contract plus real serializer/validator can prove the rule without a live socket when transport delivery is outside the claim.

sources.label: roles/verifier.md:5
sources.text: Test adequacy and code review look at the same files for different results. Check the pyramid: detailed scenarios belong at the cheapest layer that keeps the failure real, integration tests prove connections, and a few end-to-end journeys cover what only the whole system shows. Check the TDD evidence: did the intended scenario fail for its wrong behavior before it passed? A setup error is not that red, and a missing red stays a gap; never assume a run happened. Then ask whether the checks and the real-system observations tell the required behavior apart from its failures. The Reviewer judges assertions, contracts and implementation separately. Reuse adequate real-path evidence instead of repeating it to look independent. A wrong expectation is a design question for the Lead; adjusting the oracle until it goes green is never the fix.

sources.label: test-design/SKILL.md:46
sources.text: The wrong behavior sets the floor. Keep real the smallest thing responsible for it, then choose the cheapest layer that keeps it real. A mock that replaces the interaction a scenario claims leaves the claim unproven, however green the test. Take each expected outcome from the contract, a worked example, a literal or a reviewed table, never from the code under test.

sources.label: references/slice-and-proof-design.md:60
sources.text: Name an independent oracle: the expected observation comes from the obligation, not from recomputing the result with the code under test. When the repository defines proof-layer names, those names win; record the source. When it is silent, say `project silent` and use the ordinary unit, integration, smoke, and end-to-end names. When one rule covers the cases, plan a property or a table of that rule. A single example is enough only when the claim is that one case.

sources.label: principle-write-tests-that-can-fail/SKILL.md:27
sources.text: **Above the floor, choose the cheapest honest layer.** Several layers can keep the same thing real; choose among them by speed, determinism, and how clearly a failure points at the cause. Many focused tests take the detailed cases at the fastest boundary that still keeps them honest. Fewer integration tests cross real boundaries (serialization, storage, processes, protocols, components working together). A small number of end-to-end journeys cover what only the whole stack shows: startup wiring, cross-language composition, the WebView. Don't repeat every edge case at the top; when a journey finds a defect, add the cheaper regression below it. Cheapest never outranks honest, and the pyramid is a distribution, not a checklist every change must fill.
